title: Branches
subtitle: Create, switch, and manage parallel lines of work
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: You're in the middle of adding a new feature when a critical bug is reported in production. You need to fix the bug without breaking your half-finished feature.
whyItExists.solution: Branches let you work on different things simultaneously. Each branch is an independent line of commits. Switch between them instantly. Merge them when ready.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Always. Feature branches, bug fix branches, experiment branches. The rule: never commit directly to main on a shared project.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Tiny solo projects where you commit directly to main are fine. But even then, branches are free and lightweight — use them.

explainModes.beginner: A branch is like a copy of your project where you can freely make changes without affecting the original. When you're done, you merge your branch back into main.
explainModes.simple: git branch — list branches. git branch feature/login — create a branch. git switch feature/login — switch to it. git switch -c feature/login — create and switch in one step. Branches are just pointers to a commit.
explainModes.standard: HEAD is a pointer to the current branch (or directly to a commit in 'detached HEAD' state). Creating a branch is instantaneous — it just writes a new file in .git/refs/heads/. Switching branches updates your working tree files to match that branch's latest commit. Use descriptive names: feature/..., fix/..., chore/...
explainModes.technical: Branches are stored as files in .git/refs/heads/ containing just the commit hash. HEAD is in .git/HEAD, containing either 'ref: refs/heads/main' (attached) or a raw hash (detached). git switch (modern) replaced git checkout for branch switching — checkout still works but does more things. Remote tracking branches (origin/main) are read-only snapshots of the remote's state, updated by fetch/pull.
explainModes.deepDive: Git's branching model is the most powerful aspect of its design — branching is O(1) (constant time, just writes a hash). Compare to SVN where branching copies the entire codebase. Trunk-based development uses one main branch and short-lived feature branches merged frequently. Gitflow uses long-lived develop/release/hotfix branches — heavier but useful for versioned software. GitHub Flow: branch → PR → merge to main → deploy.

content.code:
# List all branches (* = current)
git branch
# * main
#   feature/dark-mode

# Create a new branch
git branch feature/user-profile

# Switch to it (modern command)
git switch feature/user-profile

# Create and switch in one step
git switch -c feature/user-profile
# (older equivalent: git checkout -b feature/user-profile)

# See all branches including remotes
git branch -a

# Delete a branch (after merging)
git branch -d feature/user-profile

# Force delete (unmerged changes — be careful)
git branch -D feature/user-profile

# 1. Start from an up-to-date main
git switch main
git pull

# 2. Create feature branch
git switch -c feature/dark-mode

# 3. Work and commit
echo '.dark { background: #000 }' >> style.css
git add style.css
git commit -m "Add dark mode base styles"

# 4. More commits...
git commit -m "Add dark mode toggle button"
git commit -m "Persist dark mode preference in localStorage"

# 5. Merge back to main (or open a Pull Request)
git switch main
git merge feature/dark-mode

# 6. Push
git push

questions.question: What does git switch -c feature/login do?
options: Creates a branch and stays on the current branch
Switches to an existing branch called feature/login
Creates a new branch called feature/login AND switches to it
Copies all files to a new folder
questions.explanation: git switch -c (or --create) creates a new branch and immediately switches to it. It's a shortcut for: git branch feature/login && git switch feature/login.

faq.q: How should I name my branches?
faq.a: Use lowercase with hyphens. Prefix by type: feature/user-auth, fix/login-redirect, chore/upgrade-deps, docs/readme-update. Many teams use issue numbers: feature/123-user-auth. Avoid spaces, dots, or special characters.

faq.q: What happens to my uncommitted changes when I switch branches?
faq.a: If the changes don't conflict with the target branch, Git carries them over (they stay in your working tree). If they conflict, Git refuses to switch — you must commit or stash them first: git stash.

examples: GitHub Flow: every change starts as a branch, gets reviewed as a PR, then merged to main
Emergency hotfix: git switch -c fix/critical-bug main → fix → PR → merge to main AND deploy
Long-running features: feature branch updated daily with git merge main to stay current
